brief.ask: Create a brand identity for Kinetra, the physiotherapy app in this folder.
brief.owner: Owner preferences: reassuring, active and professional, never clinical-cold or sporty-aggressive; for adults recovering from injury and their physiotherapists. No crosses, hearts, stick figures, spines or bones. App icons for iOS and Android, web, and a mark clinics can print.

claim.notes: Two rounds and five directions (swing, pendulum-k, joined-it, stride, tempo) produced no concept that passed the critic's cold gate, so nothing was finalized, exported, installed or put in a gallery.

concepts.title: Joined it
readsAs: a geometric-sans 'kinetra' whose i-dot has become a ball at the end of a thrown arc (bouncing-ball tittle)
the detached icon as a lowercase 'r' or desk lamp
a little figure bending forward in a stretch (stick-figure/body imagery the brief avoids)
concepts.sketchNotes: Reads as: s1 word reads cleanly as kinetra with the i's dot thrown up and right in a curve, like a ball in flight (best match to its idea); icon alone at 16 px reads as a lowercase r because the arc grows straight out of the stem. s2 a rainbow/swoosh arc over the word, the generic arc-over-the-name move; struck. s3 word ok, but the k's orange flick is fussy and the ki icon reads as kr; weaker version of s1. s4 an accented i in the word; the icon reads as a matchstick or a flame/leaf (sporty or wellness cliché); struck. s5 tr ligature is invisible below 64 px; the word reads as plain kinetra in a stock sans, so nothing to own. Keep s1. Fixes: (1) open a clear gap between the stem top and the start of the arc, so the arc leaves the i instead of growing out of it like an r shoulder; the measured merge warning confirms the risk; (2) make the flight read as a launch, rising before it falls, with the dot clearly above x-height and not level with the arc's start; (3) taper or thin the arc so the dot carries the weight, not the arc; (4) test the icon as the i plus flight at 16 px against r, and check it never reads as a raised-arm stick figure (owner exclusion); (5) keep the arc inside the word's cap height so the lockup stays compact and reassuring, not sporty.

concepts.title: Pendulum k
concepts.sketchNotes: Reads as: s1 a rounded k whose leg kicks a ball - a footballer's leg (body imagery, sporty) and a stock k with dot terminal; s2 'I/' or 'l,' - the k split into stem and detached arm, the name's initial with a cut; s3 a checkmark / letter v with a dot (UI check, different letter); s4 a plain rounded K in a stock font, generic monogram. All struck. The pendulum never reads as a pendulum because the k's arm is the only place the bob can sit, and there it becomes a kicking foot or a check. Different move for another pass: drop the letter. Draw the pendulum itself as a non-letter object with a fixed pivot at top (short hanger + one arc of travel + bob at the end of its swing, tilted in one direction) so the read is 'something in controlled motion, guided from a fixed point' (therapist as pivot). Or keep the K for the wordmark only and let the icon be the bob-on-arc. Avoid checkmark and ball-kick silhouettes.

concepts.title: Stride
concepts.sketchNotes: Reads as: s1 two scattered rounded tiles (a window/app-grid fragment); s2 the duplicate/copy icon - two identical rounded squares on a diagonal, a UI glyph; s3 a tombstone with a smaller tombstone - flat-based dome is a gravestone, fatal for a physio audience; s4 a lid popping off a box / unboxing - the only one with motion, but it reads as burst-open, not a reassuring step; s5 two capsules/pills - medication, the clinical cue the brief avoids. Common failure: two disconnected masses floating apart never read as ONE body shifting weight, so the step is invisible and the result is generic geometry (distinctiveness <=4 cold). Different move: make it a single connected form whose silhouette carries the weight shift - e.g. one soft mass with a planted flat heel and a rolled, lifted forward edge (a rocker/foot-roll profile), or two masses joined by a continuous bridge/hinge so load transfer is visible. Keep the warm orange and soft corners; drop the floating-gap composition.

concepts.title: Swing
readsAs: a letter K broken into three pieces (stem plus two petal strokes)
a figure in a lunge or kneeling stride, close to a stick-figure body
a sprouting leaf or flower opening from a stem. Unfortunate: a person collapsing onto a knee / falling, which for injury recovery is the wrong picture
concepts.sketchNotes: Reads as: s1 a stick rising out of its own motion trail, but also a fragment of a loading spinner (fading spokes); s2 three loose pills, confetti, no single object; s3 an app tile with an L / spinner cut out (stock 84%) - struck; s4 bars getting taller left to right, a signal-strength / progress-bar glyph - struck (finance-bar and UI reading). Pick s1: the only one with one confident direction of movement and a clear end state (the bar standing). Main risk is the activity-indicator reading: in development make the three bars share one visible pivot point (overlap or touch at the low-left foot, like a metronome/time-lapse of one object) so it reads as ONE bar moving, not spokes; vary length or keep the trail shorter than the final bar; avoid even angle spacing (that is what makes spinners). Keep fat rounded ends and the warm orange; drop the palest bar if it vanishes at 16 px. Watch that it does not read as an L or a check.

concepts.title: Tempo
readsAs: a UI slider/fader knob on a track
at 16-32 px a warning triangle with an exclamation mark -- the unfortunate one for an injury-recovery app
concepts.sketchNotes: Reads as: s1 a metronome, at once; s2 a pyramid / letter A with a slot, metronome lost; s3 a thin line-icon metronome (UI glyph, struck); s4 a joystick or lever on a V. Pick s1: the clearest first reading, solid body, warm accent on calm purple, outside the navy/teal set. Risks for development: (1) the music-app misreading - the stranger's first thought is a tuner/music app, so the body must feel like a calm, human object (softer radii, broader base, less instrument-like taper), not a piano accessory; (2) the orange arm is a long sharp diagonal close to a sporty slash - shorten it, lower the angle and round the ends; (3) arm and weight merged (16 px 89%) - give the weight its own silhouette with a clear gap, and check the one-colour version, where the cut-out in the body must still carry the arm; (4) the white gap currently forms an ampersand-like squiggle - clean it into one deliberate counter.
